title: US Military Uses Laser to Down Cartel Drones as Directed Energy Moves From Test to Field Use
subhead: The US military shot down three Mexican cartel drones with a high-energy laser near the border, while the Navy's top officer pushes to field directed energy weapons 'in a real way' and NATO's policy chief presses allies toward a European-led defense of the continent.

sections.heading: Directed Energy Goes Operational: Laser Downs Cartel Drones
sections.body: The US military used a high-energy laser to shoot down three Mexican drug cartel drones in southern Texas' Rio Grande Valley late Tuesday and early Wednesday, US officials said Thursday. The North American Aerospace Defense Command and US Northern Command said the operation used the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser, and that the drones posed 'a physical threat' to US military and Customs and Border Protection personnel, Reuters reports. The military did not specify the laser's manufacturer, but AeroVironment delivered its first two multi-purpose high-energy lasers to the Army last summer and has previously deployed its LOCUST system in the region. Major General Curtis Taylor, commander of Joint Task Force–Southern Border, said cartel networks are 'increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human-smuggling and actively spy on our personnel.'
sections.whyItMatters: This is a rare confirmed combat use of a directed-energy weapon against a real threat, not a test range. It signals the Army's high-energy laser program has moved from demonstration to operational employment, and it extends the counter-drone mission into the homeland-security domain.

sections.heading: Navy's 'Month of Directed Energy' Signals Fleet-Wide Push
sections.body: Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle is calling for a major push to field high-power directed energy weapons on US ships 'in a real way' to broaden fleet self-protection, previewing what he called the 'month of directed energy', Aviation Week reports from Reno, Nevada. The push comes as the Navy weighs how to defend against proliferating drone and missile threats with finite interceptor stocks. The service has tested lasers against target drones since at least April 2022, but Caudle's framing signals a shift from experimentation toward fielding decisions.
sections.whyItMatters: The Navy's top officer publicly prioritizing directed energy suggests the service is preparing procurement decisions on shipboard lasers, a segment that could reshape the naval self-defense market and pressure contractors to move from prototypes to production.

sections.heading: NATO Review: Colby Tells Allies US Wants European-Led Defense
sections.body: US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby told NATO ambassadors in Brussels on Thursday that 'in order to survive and indeed thrive, NATO must change,' and that a US review of forces in Europe is meant to 'encourage, enable, and impel a transition to a more durable and powerful European-led conventional defence of the continent,' according to prepared remarks published by the Pentagon and reported by TRT World. Washington launched a six-month review of US troop deployments in Europe in June and has sent allies a questionnaire covering defense spending, strategy, procurement and support for US foreign policy priorities. The review will produce at least four option sets for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth by November 6, ahead of a December completion deadline, per a document seen by Reuters. Diplomats described the meeting as positive but preliminary, with one European diplomat saying the message from allies was 'Europe is stepping up and unity is key.'
sections.whyItMatters: This is the clearest articulation yet of the administration's burden-shifting intent: the US is not just asking allies to spend more, but signaling it wants Europe to take the lead on its own conventional defense. The November 6 deadline gives allies a concrete timeline for spending and procurement decisions.

sections.heading: Japan Picks Terra B1 Interceptor Drone, Built on Ukraine Lessons
sections.body: Japan's Acquisition, Technology & Logistics Agency selected the Terra B1 interceptor drone for procurement after it was the only system to pass fast-track demonstration trials for the Maritime Self-Defense Force, Terra Drone announced August 25. The competition drew proposals from 38 companies, with four models reaching trials held July 15 to August 6. Japan launched the program only in June, and first deliveries could begin as early as September. The B1 is designed to counter low-cost attack drones such as the Iranian-designed Shahed family, a threat that has reshaped air defense in Ukraine. Terra Drone has partnered with Ukrainian firms Amazing Drones and WinnyLab on the related Terra A1 and A2 interceptors, which have seen operational use in Ukraine, United24 Media reports.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan is importing the interceptor-drone concept validated on the Ukrainian battlefield, where cheap drones are used to preserve expensive surface-to-air missiles. It reflects a broader shift toward cost-effective layered air defense and deepens Japan-Ukraine defense-industrial cooperation.

sections.heading: Russia Deploys Longer-Range Iskander-1000 Ballistic Missile
sections.body: Ukraine's Defense Intelligence Directorate (GUR) said Russia used the updated 9M723-2 'Iskander-1000' ballistic missile for the first time in a strike on Kyiv, with a range of up to 550 km versus about 390 km for the previous 9M723-1 variant, The War Zone reports. The longer range means launchers can sit deeper inside Russia, complicating Ukraine's new campaign to hunt ballistic missile launchers before they fire. GUR also reported that Russia has requested an additional tranche of North Korean KN-30 missiles (Hwasong-11C), though no transfer has yet been recorded. Missile expert Fabian Hoffmann estimates Russia's combined 9M723 and Kh-47M2 production capacity in mid-2026 at 600-800 units annually. GUR's War & Sanctions portal found that only a quarter of 140 components in the missiles are Russian-made, with 63 from American firms.
sections.whyItMatters: The Iskander-1000 extends Russia's strike reach and complicates Ukraine's pre-launch hunting strategy, while the foreign-component data underscores how sanctions have not severed Russia's access to Western microelectronics. It also shows Russia's missile industrial base is modernizing, not just replenishing.

sections.heading: Pentagon Industrial Base: Critical Minerals and DIBX Awards
sections.body: At the Pentagon's first Defense Industrial Base Accelerator (DIBX) event in Philadelphia, industrial base policy chief Michael Cadenazzi said critical minerals is 'front and center' as the president's 'No. 1 issue for the defense industrial base,' Defense One reports. The Pentagon has about $5 billion in reconciliation funds to invest in critical mineral supply chains through fiscal 2029, and last year took a 40 percent stake in Korea Zinc as part of a $7.4 billion move to build a processing plant in Tennessee. During the event, the Pentagon awarded six of nine companies a total of about $25 million, including 5N+ Semiconductors ($7.3 million), Graystone Resources ($6.75 million), Senra Systems ($4.4 million) and Neya Systems ($5.9 million) for autonomous fuel delivery. Private investors cited a 'duration mismatch' between long payback timelines and capital access as a barrier to critical minerals investment.
sections.whyItMatters: The Pentagon is using direct investment and small awards to seed a domestic critical minerals and advanced manufacturing base, betting that government demand signals will unlock private capital. The Korea Zinc plant, however, won't be operational for another four to five years, exposing the gap between ambition and delivery.

sections.heading: Counter-Drone Sensing Moves Onto Robotic Ground Vehicles
sections.body: L3Harris and ARX Robotics UK demonstrated the CORVUS-RAVEN counter-drone system mounted on a remotely controlled Gereon ground vehicle during the US Army's Project Convergence-Capstone 6, Defence Industry Europe reports. The passive sensing system detects signals associated with drone threats and provides bearing information, and the robotic platform lets operators extend sensing into forward or hazardous areas while staying remote. L3Harris said the open architecture and modular hardware reduced integration barriers, and lessons will inform future counter-drone deployments on robotic platforms.
sections.whyItMatters: Pairing counter-drone sensing with unmanned ground vehicles reflects the Army's push to keep personnel away from threats while extending electronic warfare coverage — a pattern that could drive demand for modular robotic platforms carrying EW and counter-UAS payloads.

bottomLine: Directed energy crossed a threshold this week: the US military used a laser to down real cartel drones near the border, and the Navy's top officer is pushing to field shipboard lasers 'in a real way.' That operational turn, alongside Japan's fast-track adoption of a Ukraine-proven interceptor drone and Russia's fielding of the longer-range Iskander-1000, shows the counter-drone and missile-modernization races are accelerating on multiple fronts. Meanwhile, the Pentagon's NATO review crystallized into a concrete demand for European-led defense with a November 6 deadline, and the industrial base push for critical minerals moved from policy talk to small-dollar awards. The through-line: cost-effective, layered defense against cheap threats is becoming the organizing principle of procurement, and the US is leaning on allies and industry to carry more of the burden.
sources: Reuters (via USA Today), Aviation Week, TRT World, United24 Media, The War Zone, Defense One, Defence Industry Europe
